Compute the largest positive integer \( n \) such that

\[
n \text{ divides } (\lfloor \sqrt{n} \rfloor)!^{n!} + 450.
\]

Put your final answer within \boxed{}.

message.content:
Let

\[
k=\lfloor \sqrt n\rfloor ,\qquad A=(k!)^{n!}.
\]

So \(k^2\le n<(k+1)^2\). We classify the prime powers that can divide \(n\).

---

### 1. Primes \(p\le k\)

Suppose \(p^a\|\!n\) and \(p\le k\). Then \(p\mid k!\), so

\[
v_p(A)=n!\,v_p(k!)\ge n!\ge n\ge a.
\]

Thus \(A\equiv 0\pmod{p^a}\). Since \(n\mid A+450\), we must have

\[
p^a\mid 450.
\]

Hence any prime power of \(n\) whose prime is \(\le k\) must divide

\[
450=2\cdot 3^2\cdot 5^2.
\]

---

### 2. Primes \(p>k\)

Suppose \(p\mid n\) and \(p>k\). Since \(p\ge k+1\),

\[
p^2\ge (k+1)^2>n,
\]

so \(p\|\!n\).

Also \(p\nmid k!\). Because \(p\le n\), the integer \(p-1\) appears as a factor of \(n!\), so

\[
p-1\mid n!.
\]

By Fermat’s little theorem,

\[
(k!)^{p-1}\equiv 1\pmod p,
\]

so

\[
A=(k!)^{n!}\equiv 1\pmod p.
\]

Since \(p\mid A+450\), we get

\[
p\mid 1+450=451.
\]

But

\[
451=11\cdot 41.
\]

Therefore any prime divisor of \(n\) that is larger than \(k\) must be \(11\) or \(41\).

---

### 3. Bounding \(n\)

From the two cases:

- primes \(\le k\) can only contribute prime powers dividing \(450\);
- primes \(>k\) can only be \(11\) or \(41\), each to the first power;
- \(n\) cannot contain both \(11\) and \(41\), since then both would have to be \(>k\), forcing \(k\le 10\) and \(n<121\), impossible because \(11\cdot 41=451\mid n\).

Now consider whether \(41\mid n\).

If \(41\nmid n\), then either \(11\mid n\) or neither \(11\) nor \(41\) divides \(n\).

- If \(11\mid n\), then \(11>k\), so \(k\le 10\) and \(n<121\), hence \(n\le 120\).
- If neither divides \(n\), then every prime power of \(n\) divides \(450\), so \(n\mid 450\), hence \(n\le 450\).

Thus if \(41\nmid n\), then \(n\le 450\).

If \(41\mid n\), then \(41>k\), so \(k\le 40\). Hence

\[
n<(41)^2=1681.
\]

Write \(n=41m\). The remaining part \(m\) can only contain prime powers dividing \(450\), so \(m\mid 450\). Also

\[
m=\frac{n}{41}<41.
\]

The largest divisor of \(450\) less than \(41\) is \(30\). Therefore

\[
n=41m\le 41\cdot 30=1230.
\]

So every valid \(n\) satisfies \(n\le 1230\).

---

### 4. Verification that \(n=1230\) works

For \(n=1230\),

\[
\lfloor \sqrt{1230}\rfloor=35,
\]

and

\[
1230=30\cdot 41.
\]

Modulo \(30\): since \(30\mid 35!\) and \(30\mid 450\),

\[
(35!)^{1230!}+450\equiv 0+0\equiv 0\pmod{30}.
\]

Modulo \(41\): since \(41\nmid 35!\) and \(40\mid 1230!\), Fermat gives

\[
(35!)^{1230!}\equiv 1\pmod{41}.
\]

Also \(450\equiv -1\pmod{41}\) because \(451=11\cdot 41\). Hence

\[
(35!)^{1230!}+450\equiv 1-1\equiv 0\pmod{41}.
\]

Since \(\gcd(30,41)=1\), we get

\[
1230\mid (35!)^{1230!}+450.
\]

Therefore the largest such positive integer is

\[
\boxed{1230}.
\]
